statement: The variance of a random variable X is a measure of dispersion defined as the expected value of the squared deviation from the mean: \operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}\left[(X - \operatorname{E}[X])^2\right].

symbols.meaning: expected value or mean of X (often denoted \mu)

properties.why: variance equals the mean of the square minus the square of the mean
squared deviations are positive or zero
a constant does not deviate from its mean

properties.property: Almost sure constancy: \operatorname{Var}(X) = 0 \iff \exists a : P(X = a) = 1
properties.why: a random variable with zero variance always takes the same value almost surely
standard deviation is defined as the square root of the variance
evaluating expectation with respect to probability mass function p_i

properties.property: Continuous random variable form: \operatorname{Var}(X) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} (x - \mu)^2 f(x)\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}} x^2 f(x)\,dx - \mu^2
properties.why: evaluating expectation with respect to probability density function f(x)

properties.property: Pairwise difference formulation for n equally likely values: \operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_i \sum_{j > i} (x_i - x_j)^2
properties.why: variance expressed in terms of squared distances of points without referring to the mean

properties.property: Law of total variance: \operatorname{Var}[X] = \operatorname{E}(\operatorname{Var}[X \mid Y]) + \operatorname{Var}(\operatorname{E}[X \mid Y])
properties.why: variance decomposes across conditioning on another random variable Y

assumptions.breaks_when: The distribution lacks a finite expected value (e.g., Cauchy distribution)
The second moment diverges even if the expected value is finite (e.g., Pareto distribution with index 1 < k \le 2)

failure_modes.signature: \operatorname{Var}(X) fails to exist or diverges to infinity
failure_modes.cause: Underlying distribution lacks a finite mean or possesses an infinite second moment

failure_modes.signature: Severe loss of precision or negative variance values
failure_modes.cause: Using \operatorname{E}[X^2] - \operatorname{E}[X]^2 when the two components are of similar magnitude
